title: Pluscuamperfecto / Past Perfect (past of the past)
bridge: In Pulaar, the past perfect (often called 'past of the past') is used to express an action that happened before another past action, similar to Spanish's pluscuamperfecto. In English, the past perfect (had eaten) serves the same function, but there are key differences: word order is fixed ('had' + past participle), and English frequently uses 'already', 'just', 'never' to emphasize sequence. Be careful: in Spanish, the preterite (comí) is sometimes used where English requires the past perfect (had eaten) when the earlier action is clear. In Pulaar, the past perfect is formed with the auxiliary 'wo' (had) + the past participle of the main verb.
rule: The past perfect is formed with the auxiliary 'wo' (for all persons) + the past participle of the main verb. It is used to express an action that occurred before another past action, i.e., the 'past of the past'. In affirmative sentences: subject + wo + past participle. In negative sentences: wo + not (woot) + past participle. In questions: Wo + subject + past participle. It is used with time markers like 'hokku', 'jokko', 'wona', 'hokku', 'na', 'hore'. Examples: 'Mi woot jappi miɗo na teew' (I had finished my work before dinner). It is also used in indirect speech to shift a verb tense back (present perfect -> past perfect). Exception: in English, 'after' and 'before' sometimes allow the simple past if the order is obvious, but the past perfect provides clarity. Note: in Pulaar, the past perfect is used more restrictively; in English, it is common in narratives to establish the order of events.

concept_examples.text: She had already left when I arrived.
concept_examples.translation: O yimɓe woot jappi na mi yahii.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ʃiː hæd ɔːlˈrɛdi lɛft wɛn aɪ əˈraɪvd/

concept_examples.text: They had never seen such a beautiful sunset before.
concept_examples.translation: Hoon en wonaa jappi sappo e nden.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ðeɪ hæd ˈnɛvər siːn sʌtʃ ə ˈbjuːtəfəl ˈsʌnsɛt bɪˈfɔːr/

concept_examples.text: By the time we got to the station, the train had already departed.
concept_examples.translation: Na mi yahii laawol, teew o woot jappi.
concept_examples.phonetic: /baɪ ðə taɪm wiː gɒt tə ðə ˈsteɪʃən, ðə treɪn hæd ɔːlˈrɛdi dɪˈpɑːrtɪd/

concept_examples.text: He had studied English for years before moving to London.
concept_examples.translation: O woot jappi innglese fof fowtaade mawnde London.
concept_examples.phonetic: /hiː hæd ˈstʌdid ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ fɔːr jɪərz bɪˈfɔːr ˈmuːvɪŋ tə ˈlʌndən/

common_error.wrong: When I arrived, she already left.
common_error.correct: When I arrived, she had already left.
common_error.correct_alt: She had already left when I arrived.
common_error.explanation: In Pulaar, it is common to use the simple past (o jappi) for the earlier action, but in English, to indicate that an action occurred before another in the past, you need the past perfect (had + past participle). The clue is the context: the action of 'leaving' occurred before 'arriving', so 'had left' is used. To avoid this, identify which action is earlier and put it in past perfect; the later action in simple past.

examples.original: I had finished my work.
examples.phonetic: /aɪ hæd ˈfɪnɪʃt maɪ wɜːrk/
examples.translation: Mi woot jappi miɗo.
examples.note: Affirmative: subject + wo + past participle. The past participle of regular verbs ends in -i.

examples.original: She hadn't seen the movie before.
examples.phonetic: /ʃiː ˈhædənt siːn ðə ˈmuːvi bɪˈfɔːr/
examples.translation: O woota jappi film nden.
examples.note: Negative: wo + not (woot) + past participle. Note the contraction.

examples.original: Had you ever visited Paris?
examples.phonetic: /hæd juː ˈɛvər ˈvɪzɪtɪd ˈpærɪs/
examples.translation: Hoon woota jappi Pari naa?
examples.note: Question: Wo + subject + past participle. 'naa' is used in questions to indicate 'ever'.

levels.label: Sequence of events: past perfect + past simple
levels.translation: Sequence of events: past perfect + simple past

examples.original: After they had eaten, they went for a walk.
examples.phonetic: /ˈæftər ðeɪ hæd ˈiːtən, ðeɪ wɛnt fɔːr ə wɔːk/
examples.translation: Hore en woot jappi, en yahii naaɗa.
examples.note: The earlier action (eating) is in past perfect; the later action (going for a walk) in simple past.

examples.original: The party had started before we arrived.
examples.phonetic: /ðə ˈpɑːrti hæd ˈstɑːrtɪd bɪˈfɔːr wiː əˈraɪvd/
examples.translation: Festa o woot jappi na mi yahii.
examples.note: With 'before', past perfect is used for the action that occurred first.

examples.original: By the time he called, I had already gone to bed.
examples.phonetic: /baɪ ðə taɪm hiː kɔːld, aɪ hæd ɔːlˈrɛdi gɒn tə bɛd/
examples.translation: Na mi yahii, mi woota jappi naaɗa.
examples.note: The expression 'by the time' + simple past requires past perfect in the other clause.

examples.original: She was upset because she had just lost her keys.
examples.phonetic: /ʃiː wʌz ʌpˈsɛt bɪˈkɔːz ʃiː hæd dʒʌst lɔːst hɜːr kiːz/
examples.translation: O yahii tobbinaa no mbii teew.
examples.note: 'Just' is placed between 'wo' and the past participle. It is equivalent to 'acabar de' in Spanish.

examples.original: I realized I had never tried sushi before that day.
examples.phonetic: /aɪ ˈrɪəlaɪzd aɪ hæd ˈnɛvər traɪd ˈsuːʃi bɪˈfɔːr ðæt deɪ/
examples.translation: Mi yahii tobbinaa no mbii sappo e nden.
examples.note: 'Never' is used in negative sentences to indicate that something had never happened.

examples.original: They had already finished the project when the boss arrived.
examples.phonetic: /ðeɪ hæd ɔːlˈrɛdi ˈfɪnɪʃt ðə ˈprɒdʒɛkt wɛn ðə bɒs əˈraɪvd/
examples.translation: Hoon en woota jappi proje naaɗa na mi yahii laawol.
examples.note: With 'already', it emphasizes that the earlier action was completed.

title: Conditionals Type 1 and 2 / Condicionales 1 e 2
bridge: In Pulaar, we use the subjunctive mood in the conditional clause and the simple conditional in the main clause (Si mi yimɓe, mi yahay). In English, the structure is different: in the first conditional we use the simple present in the 'if' clause and 'will' + base verb in the main clause. In the second conditional, we use the simple past in the 'if' clause and 'would' + base verb in the main clause. Be careful: in English, the simple past in the second conditional does not indicate past time, but a hypothetical or unreal situation in the present or future. Avoid the mistake of translating literally from Pulaar, because the structures are different.
rule: The first conditional (type 1) is used for real or possible situations in the present or future. It is formed with: If + subject + verb in simple present, + subject + will + base verb. Example: If it rains, we will stay at home. The 'if' clause can go at the beginning or at the end, and when it comes first, it is separated by a comma. You can also use 'unless' (unless) instead of 'if not'. The second conditional (type 2) is used for hypothetical, unlikely, or unreal situations in the present or future. It is formed with: If + subject + verb in simple past, + subject + would + base verb. Example: If I had more money, I would travel. In the second conditional, the verb 'to be' is used with 'were' for all persons (If I were...). 'Was' is not used in a formal context, although in informal English it is sometimes used. You can also use 'could' or 'might' instead of 'would' to express possibility or ability. The second conditional is used to give advice ('If I were you, I would...') and to express imaginary wishes.

concept_examples.text: If I study, I will pass the exam.
concept_examples.translation: If I study, I will pass the exam.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ ˈstʌdi aɪ wɪl pæs ðə ɪɡˈzæm/

concept_examples.text: If she calls you, tell her I am busy.
concept_examples.translation: If she calls you, tell her I am busy.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɪf ʃi kɔːlz ju tɛl hɜr aɪ æm ˈbɪzi/

concept_examples.text: If I were rich, I would buy a house.
concept_examples.translation: If I were rich, I would buy a house.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ wɜr rɪtʃ aɪ wʊd baɪ ə haʊs/

concept_examples.text: What would you do if you won the lottery?
concept_examples.translation: What would you do if you won the lottery?
concept_examples.phonetic: /wʌt wʊd ju duː ɪf ju wʌn ðə ˈlɑːtəri/

common_error.wrong: If I would have time, I will go to the party.
common_error.correct: If I have time, I will go to the party.
common_error.correct_alt: If I had time, I would go to the party.
common_error.explanation: In English, 'would' is never used in the 'if' clause of type 1 and 2 conditionals. In Pulaar, we sometimes say 'si mi yahay', but in English the conditional clause takes the simple present (type 1) or simple past (type 2). To avoid this mistake, remember that 'would' only appears in the main clause. If you want to express a real future possibility, use the first conditional; if it is hypothetical, use the second.

examples.original: If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.
examples.phonetic: /ɪf ɪt reɪnz wi wɪl ˈkænsəl ðə ˈpɪknɪk/
examples.translation: If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.
examples.note: We use simple present after 'if' and 'will' in the main clause.

examples.original: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
examples.phonetic: /ənˈlɛs ju ˈhʌri ju wɪl mɪs ðə bʌs/
examples.translation: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
examples.note: 'Unless' means 'if not' and already includes the negation, so 'not' is not used after it.

examples.original: If we don't leave now, we'll be late.
examples.phonetic: /ɪf wi doʊnt liːv naʊ wil bi leɪt/
examples.translation: If we don’t leave now, we will arrive late.
examples.note: Contraction 'we'll' for 'we will'. In the if clause we use present with negation.

examples.original: If I had a car, I would drive to work.
examples.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ hæd ə kɑr aɪ wʊd draɪv tuː wɜrk/
examples.translation: If I had a car, I would go to work by car.
examples.note: Simple past 'had' in the if clause, even though it refers to the present or future.

examples.original: If she were here, she would know what to do.
examples.phonetic: /ɪf ʃi wɜr hɪr ʃi wʊd noʊ wʌt tuː duː/
examples.translation: If she were here, she would know what to do.
examples.note: We use 'were' (not 'was') for all persons in formal contexts.

examples.original: If we won the match, we would be champions.
examples.phonetic: /ɪf wi wʌn ðə mætʃ wi wʊd bi ˈtʃæmpiənz/
examples.translation: If we won the match, we would be champions.
examples.note: The simple past 'won' does not indicate past time, but an unlikely condition.

examples.original: If I were you, I would apologize.
examples.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ wɜr ju aɪ wʊd əˈpɑləˌdʒaɪz/
examples.translation: If I were you, I would apologize.
examples.note: Common expression to give advice: 'If I were you, ...'

examples.original: If we had more time, we could visit the museum.
examples.phonetic: /ɪf wi hæd mɔr taɪm wi kʊd ˈvɪzɪt ðə mjuˈziːəm/
examples.translation: If we had more time, we could visit the museum.
examples.note: 'Could' in the main clause expresses possibility or ability.

examples.original: If they invited me, I might go to the party.
examples.phonetic: /ɪf ðeɪ ɪnˈvaɪtɪd mi aɪ maɪt goʊ tuː ðə ˈpɑrti/
examples.translation: If they invited me, I might go to the party.
examples.note: 'Might' indicates less possibility than 'would', similar to 'maybe'.

title: Passive Voice: Present & Past / Ndiyam fofa: haaɗe e haaɗe mawɗe
bridge: En Pulaar, la voz pasiva se forma con 'wonaa' + participio, igual que en inglés (to be + past participle). Sin embargo, en inglés el complemento agente se introduce con 'by', mientras que en Pulaar usamos 'e' o 'naa'. Además, en inglés el sujeto de la pasiva recibe más énfasis que en Pulaar, donde a menudo se prefiere la voz activa o la pasiva refleja ('se' o 'wonaa'). Un error común es omitir el verbo 'wonaa' o confundir la forma del participio pasado.
rule: La voz pasiva se forma con el verbo 'wonaa' en el tiempo correspondiente (presente simple: wonaa; pasado simple: wonii) + el participio pasado del verbo principal. El sujeto de la oración activa pasa a ser complemento agente con 'e' o 'naa' (aunque puede omitirse si no es importante). Para formar la pasiva, el objeto de la activa se convierte en sujeto. Ejemplos: Active: 'The chef cooks the meal' → Passive: 'The meal is cooked by the chef' → 'Daaɗo wonii fofa e ndiyam'. En presente, usamos 'wonaa'. En pasado, 'wonii'. El participio pasado es la tercera forma del verbo (regular: -a; irregular: lista). Excepciones: no se usa pasiva con verbos intransitivos (no llevan objeto). Uso típico: cuando el agente es desconocido, obvio o menos importante que la acción.

concept_examples.text: English is spoken all over the world.
concept_examples.phonetic: /ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ ɪz ˈspoʊkən ɔːl ˈoʊvər ðə wɜːrld/
/ðə haʊs wɒz bɪlt ɪn naɪnˈtiːn naɪnti/

concept_examples.text: These shoes are made in Italy.
concept_examples.translation: Daaɗe nden wonii fofa e Itale.

common_error.correct_alt: The house was built in 1990 by the builders.
common_error.explanation: El error ocurre porque en Pulaar usamos el infinitivo o el participio de forma similar, pero en inglés el participio pasado de los verbos irregulares no es igual al infinitivo. 'Build' es el infinitivo, 'built' es el participio pasado. Para evitar este error, memoriza la lista de verbos irregulares y practica la forma del participio. También es común olvidar el verbo 'wonaa' en la pasiva, por ejemplo: 'The house built in 1990' (incorrecto) → 'Daaɗo fofa e 1990' (incorrecto). Recuerda que siempre necesitas 'wonii/wonaa' + participio.

examples.original: The coffee is made with fresh beans.
examples.phonetic: /ðə ˈkɔːfi ɪz ˈmeɪd wɪð frɛʃ biːnz/
examples.translation: Kafe wonii fofa e ndiyam mawɗe.
examples.note: En presente, usamos 'wonaa' con sujetos singulares y 'wonaa' con plurales.

examples.original: These books are read by many students.
examples.phonetic: /ðiːz bʊks ɑːr rɛd baɪ ˈmɛni ˈstuːdənts/
examples.translation: Daaɗe nden wonii fofa e ndamɗe mawɗe.
examples.note: El agente se introduce con 'e'. En Pulaar decimos 'e' o 'naa'.

examples.original: The window is cleaned every week.
examples.phonetic: /ðə ˈwɪndoʊ ɪz kliːnd ˈɛvri wiːk/
examples.translation: Daaɗo wonii fofa e yimɓe.
examples.note: En Pulaar usamos la pasiva refleja 'wonaa' más que la pasiva con 'ser'.

examples.original: The movie was directed by Spielberg.
examples.phonetic: /ðə ˈmuːvi wɒz dɪˈrɛktɪd baɪ ˈspiːlbɜːrɡ/
examples.translation: Filmi wonii fofa e Spielberg.
examples.note: Usamos 'wonii' con sujetos singulares en pasado.

examples.original: The cookies were baked by my grandmother.
examples.phonetic: /ðə ˈkʊkiz wɜːr beɪkt baɪ maɪ ˈɡrænˌmʌðər/
examples.translation: Kooki wonii fofa e baaba mbabba.
examples.note: 'Wonii' se usa con sujetos plurales.

examples.original: The letter was written in Spanish.
examples.phonetic: /ðə ˈlɛtər wɒz ˈrɪtən ɪn ˈspænɪʃ/
examples.translation: Daaɗo wonii fofa e Fulfulde.
examples.note: El participio de 'write' es 'written' (irregular).

examples.original: The car was stolen last night.
examples.phonetic: /ðə kɑːr wɒz ˈstoʊlən læst naɪt/
examples.translation: El coche fue robado anoche.
examples.note: No mencionamos 'by someone' porque es desconocido o irrelevante.

examples.original: Rice is grown in many countries.
examples.phonetic: /raɪs ɪz groʊn ɪn ˈmɛni ˈkʌntriz/
examples.translation: El arroz se cultiva en muchos países.
examples.note: El agente es general, no necesitamos especificarlo.

examples.original: The tests are graded by the teacher.
examples.phonetic: /ðə tɛsts ɑːr ˈɡreɪdɪd baɪ ðə ˈtiːtʃər/
examples.translation: Los exámenes son calificados por el profesor.
examples.note: Aquí sí se incluye el agente porque es importante.
